<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-summary">Summary</button></h2><div id="work-acc-summary" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Ratnāvalī is a Sanskrit play set in the kingdom of Ujjayinī, where King Udayana falls in love with Ratnāvalī, the princess of a neighboring kingdom. The play unfolds as King Udayana, aided by his clever friend Vasantaka, tries to win Ratnāvalī's heart.<br><br>The story begins with King Udayana's search for a suitable bride. He is advised by his ministers to marry Ratnāvalī, the princess of the kingdom of Simhala. Despite initial reluctance, Udayana sets out to win her over, disguised as a gardener. Vasantaka, who is in love with the queen's maid, Madanikā, accompanies him on this mission.<br><br>Using his wit and charm, Udayana succeeds in getting close to Ratnāvalī, and they fall in love. However, their happiness is short-lived as the king of Simhala demands that Ratnāvalī marry a prince from his own kingdom. Udayana, with the help of Vasantaka and Madanikā, devises a plan to rescue Ratnāvalī and bring her back to Ujjayinī.<br><br>The play features elements of comedy, romance, and drama, and is known for its clever wordplay and lyrical language. It explores themes of love, friendship, loyalty, and the challenges of political and social conventions. The play ends with the marriage of Udayana and Ratnāvalī, and the union of Vasantaka and Madanikā.<br><br>Ratnāvalī is considered one of the finest examples of Sanskrit drama and is still performed today in various parts of India. Its enduring popularity can be attributed to its engaging plot, memorable characters, and poetic language.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contents">Contents</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contents" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Act 1: The King's Dilemma<br><br>Introduction of King Udayana and his court<br>King Udayana's search for a suitable bride<br>Introduction of Ratnāvalī, the princess of Simhala<br>King Udayana's initial reluctance to marry Ratnāvalī<br><br>Act 2: The King's Disguise<br><br>King Udayana's decision to win Ratnāvalī's heart<br>Udayana disguises himself as a gardener and visits Simhala<br>Vasantaka accompanies Udayana and falls in love with Madanikā, a maid in Ratnāvalī's court<br><br>Act 3: The Lovers' Meeting<br><br>Udayana's meeting with Ratnāvalī in the garden<br>Udayana's and Ratnāvalī's growing love for each other<br>Vasantaka's attempts to win over Madanikā<br><br>Act 4: The King's Demand<br><br>The king of Simhala demands that Ratnāvalī marry a prince from his own kingdom<br>Udayana and Vasantaka plan to rescue Ratnāvalī<br>Madanikā helps them in their plan<br><br>Act 5: The Escape<br><br>Udayana, Vasantaka, and Ratnāvalī's escape from Simhala<br>The pursuit of Udayana and Ratnāvalī by the king of Simhala's army<br>Vasantaka's bravery in defending Ratnāvalī<br><br>Act 6: The Reunion<br><br>Udayana and Ratnāvalī's reunion in Ujjayinī<br>The marriage of Udayana and Ratnāvalī<br>The union of Vasantaka and Madanikā<br>Ratnāvalī is a five-act play written in Sanskrit and is known for its engaging plot, memorable characters, and poetic language. It explores themes of love, friendship, loyalty, and the challenges of political and social conventions.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-uniqueness">Uniqueness</button></h2><div id="work-acc-uniqueness" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Ratnāvalī is considered unique in Sanskrit literature for several reasons. One of the most notable is its use of Prākrit language and idioms, which were commonly used in everyday speech during that time, making it more relatable and accessible to the common people. The play also incorporates elements of music, dance, and drama, which were popular forms of entertainment in ancient India. Additionally, Ratnāvalī is notable for its portrayal of women, who are depicted as strong, intelligent, and capable of making their own decisions, which was a departure from the traditional gender roles of that era.</div></div></div>
<div class="accordion-item"><h2 class="accordion-header"><button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#work-acc-contribution">Contribution &amp; Notes</button></h2><div id="work-acc-contribution" class="accordion-collapse collapse"><div class="accordion-body">Ratnāvalī represents a shift towards a more accessible and relatable style of writing, which was in contrast to the highly stylized and formal language of earlier Sanskrit literature. This style of writing made the play more popular and helped to expand the audience for Sanskrit literature beyond the traditional scholarly circles.<br><br>Ratnāvalī is one of the few surviving examples of Sanskrit drama, and it is considered a significant work in the history of Indian theatre. The play's influence can be seen in the works of later Sanskrit playwrights, as well as in the development of regional theatre traditions throughout India.<br><br>One interesting aspect of Ratnāvalī is its use of a frame story, which is a narrative structure in which a secondary story serves as a vehicle for telling the main story. In the case of Ratnāvalī, the frame story involves a king who has lost his beloved queen and is comforted by a jester who tells him the story of Ratnāvalī and her love for the king's son.<br><br>The play also contains a number of musical interludes, which are meant to be sung or chanted by the actors on stage. These musical interludes serve to heighten the emotional impact of the play and are an important part of its overall structure.</div></div></div>
